title: Bell and Harvest
premise: Emrys Dunmore, a hospice nurse who has spent years rationalizing the backwards counting they hear from the dying, returns to their late grandmother's farmhouse in the frostbitten hollow of Harrow's Bend and finds Wren, the imaginary friend they buried at age nine, waiting on the porch — unchanged, adult-shaped, and terrified. The village bell that hasn't rung since Emrys's childhood begins to toll each nightfall, marking off hours until the first hard frost, when whatever was invited in decades ago by Emrys's grandmother will come to collect what remains of the family line. Over one long night, with Wren, the skeptical local priest Father Idris, and the last surviving harvest family, Emrys must uncover the truth: their grandmother bargained the village's deaths for her own child's life, and the debt now falls to Emrys. In the end, Emrys refuses both sacrifice and escape, instead breaking the bargain by naming the thing honestly before dawn — unmaking it at the cost of Wren's existence, and choosing to grieve a found family rather than inherit a corrupted power.
about_author: Z. M. Lockridge is the pen name of a former rural hospice volunteer who grew up in farming country where old bells still hung in disused chapels. They write horror about tenderness under pressure, insisting that the scariest houses are the ones someone loved enough to protect.

chapters.title: The Counting Ward
chapters.summary: Emrys's POV. At the hospice, Mr. Aldery counts down from thirty as he dies, and Emrys documents it clinically in a private notebook, refusing the word 'omen.' The emotional beat is controlled denial — competence as armor against a pattern they can no longer ignore.

chapters.title: Letter Written in Frost
chapters.summary: Emrys's POV. A solicitor's letter summons them to Harrow's Bend: grandmother Maren Dunmore is dead, the house is theirs, and the will insists Emrys arrive 'before the frost.' Emrys resents being managed even by the dead; grief curdles into suspicion.

chapters.title: What Waited on the Porch
chapters.summary: Emrys's POV. Arriving at dusk, Emrys finds Wren on the porch — the imaginary friend, unchanged after twenty years, now wearing a body like an ill-fitting coat. The beat is vertigo: the impossible made domestic, and Emrys's disbelief cracking at its first seam.

chapters.title: Housekeeping for Ghosts
chapters.summary: Wren's POV. Wren explains they've kept the house 'tidy' since Maren died — salt lines renewed, mirrors covered — and begs Emrys not to unpack the attic. Emotional beat: desperate caretaking masking terror, and the first hint that Wren knows exactly what was invited in.

chapters.title: The Bell That Forgot Itself
chapters.summary: Father Idris's POV. The chapel bell rings once at nightfall though its rope rotted decades ago. Idris, a rationalist priest, logs it like weather data. Beat: institutional skepticism beginning to fail as the whole village pretends not to hear.

chapters.title: Harvest Families
chapters.summary: Emrys's POV. At the village store, the Ollerenshaw sisters warn Emrys away from the fields after dark and mention, casually, that everyone's clocks run fast this week. Beat: small-town complicity — a community that has survived by not asking questions.

chapters.title: Attic, Sealed
chapters.summary: Wren's POV. Wren physically blocks the attic door and finally admits Maren made a bargain long ago — a life traded for a life — but claims not to know the terms. Beat: betrayal and tenderness tangled; Emrys realizes Wren may be part of the payment.

chapters.title: Backwards From Nine
chapters.summary: Emrys's POV. Flashback interleave: age nine, the fever, the counting voice under the floorboards, and how Wren appeared the morning Emrys recovered while another child in the hollow sickened. Beat: the horror of realizing survival itself may have been purchased.

chapters.title: Salt and Small Mercies
chapters.summary: Father Idris's POV. Idris visits the house, tests the thresholds, and finds consecrated ground simply ends at the property line, like a fence. He chooses to stay anyway. Beat: duty versus compassion — his first step toward found family.

chapters.title: The First Toll
chapters.summary: Multiple brief POVs braided. The bell tolls thirteen times; frost ferns bloom across every window facing the fields; the Ollerenshaws' eldest doesn't come home from checking the cider press. Beat: dread going public — the village can no longer pretend.

chapters.title: Ledger of the Hollow
chapters.summary: Emrys's POV. In Maren's effects, Emrys finds a ledger: names, dates, and columns of counted-down numbers matching the hospice notebook — including Maren's own final entry, unfinished. Beat: cold clarity; the denial structure collapses entirely.

chapters.title: Wren, Unchanged
chapters.summary: Wren's POV. Wren confesses they are not a friend but a remainder — the piece of whatever was invited in that learned to love Emrys and hid inside childhood. Beat: devastating honesty; love revealed as possibly a lure, possibly the only true thing.

chapters.title: Terms of Invitation
chapters.summary: Father Idris's POV. Deciphering Maren's ledger with parish archives, Idris reconstructs the bargain: Maren invited something old into the hollow to save dying Emrys, and it has fed on the village's dead ever since, collecting fully at each generation's first hard frost. Beat: power's inheritance — Emrys owns the debt by blood.

chapters.title: The Offer
chapters.summary: Emrys's POV. At midnight the thing speaks through the frost itself, offering Emrys the same deal Maren took: name a substitute, live freely, hold the power of the ledger. Beat: temptation rendered intimate — it offers to spare Wren if Emrys becomes the next Maren.

chapters.title: What Duty Costs
chapters.summary: Idris's POV. Idris argues Emrys must take the bargain to end the cycle cleanly — one corrupted keeper beats endless feeding. Emrys refuses; Wren sides with Idris against their own existence. Beat: love against duty fracturing the fragile found family.

chapters.title: Frostline
chapters.summary: Emrys's POV. The temperature plummets; the bell tolls without pause; the fields fill with shapes wearing the faces of everyone the ledger recorded. The group fortifies the kitchen as the house's protections burn out one by one. Beat: siege horror, courage measured in minutes.

chapters.title: The Pattern Writes Itself
chapters.summary: Wren's POV. On the frosted window, the frost forms the original contract's signature — Maren's, and beneath it, forming letter by letter, Emrys's. Wren realizes the invitation completes itself unless named aloud. Beat: race-against-dawn urgency and self-sacrifice surfacing.

chapters.title: Naming It
chapters.summary: Emrys's POV. Climax. As frost reaches Emrys's lips, they do what neither Maren nor the thing expected: speak its true nature aloud — not its name, but the truth of what it is, a hunger dressed as mercy — refusing the categories of bargain, debt, and heirloom. Beat: defiance as exorcism; language as the only weapon left.

chapters.title: Sunrise Arithmetic
chapters.summary: Multiple POVs. The thing unravels backward through its own counting, taking the ledger, the bell's voice, and Wren with it. Emrys holds Wren as they thin into morning light. Beat: climax's cost — victory inseparable from loss.

chapters.title: After the Harvest
chapters.summary: Idris's POV. Days later: clocks run true, the hospice-style counting stops, and the village awkwardly begins telling the truth to one another. Idris buries the chapel bell's rope with honors. Beat: communal healing, quiet and unsentimental.

chapters.title: Grief With a Name
chapters.summary: Emrys's POV. Emrys stays in the house, nurses the dying again — and hears silence where the counting used to be, which is its own kind of ache. They set a place at the table for Wren. Beat: mourning a found family member no one else remembers.

chapters.title: Bell and Harvest
chapters.summary: Emrys's POV, coda. A year later, on the first frost night, Emrys rings the restored bell once — not a summons, but a memorial — and finds a single perfect frost fern on the porch glass shaped, impossibly, like a wave goodbye. Beat: bittersweet resolution; love outlasting the thing that borrowed its shape.
